common_name: Bull's Blood Beet (Deep Crimson Heirloom Beet with Dark Ornamental Foliage)

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep as soon as soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; in zone 9, Bull's Blood grows best September through April, as summer heat pushes it to bolt quickly.

directions: Direct sow beet 'seeds' (actually dried seed clusters) 1/2 inch deep, thinning to one seedling per cluster once true leaves appear. Bull's Blood is an 1840s heirloom grown as much for its intensely dark maroon-red foliage as for its roots, and the young leaves are the main draw for cooks and flower arrangers alike, prized as a striking baby-leaf salad green and garnish that holds its deep color even when lightly cooked. The roots themselves are smaller and more fibrous than modern table-beet varieties, sweet but best pulled young rather than left to bulk up. Sow it thickly for a continuous cut-and-come-again crop of colorful microgreens and baby leaves, or thin selectively and let some roots mature for classic beet flavor with a dramatic garden presence.
sources: Cornell Cooperative Extension — Beet Variety Notes

common_name: Golden Globe Turnip (Classic Sweet Yellow-Fleshed Heirloom Turnip)

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep 6–10 weeks before the first fall frost for the sweetest roots, or as early as the soil can be worked in late winter; in zone 9, an October sowing usually outperforms a spring one since the roots size up in cool, mild weather without bolting.

directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to 3–4 inches apart once seedlings have their first true leaves, using the thinnings as tender salad greens. Golden Globe is a 19th-century English heirloom valued for its smooth, golden-skinned, yellow-fleshed roots, which are noticeably sweeter and milder than white-fleshed turnips and hold good texture even when they size up past baseball size. It bulks up quickly from a compact top, making it a good choice for close spacing and succession sowing, and the mild flavor suits it equally well to roasting, mashing, or eating raw and thinly sliced. Keep soil evenly moist for fast, uninterrupted growth, since checks from drought or heat toughen the roots and sharpen their flavor.

common_name: Mexico Midget Tomato (Tiny-Fruited Heirloom Currant Tomato)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50°F; in zone 9, set out in March for a spring crop and again in July for a heavy fall crop that runs until frost.

directions: Transplant into warm soil after all danger of frost, staking or caging the sprawling vines since a single plant can carry hundreds of tiny fruit clusters by midsummer. Mexico Midget is a wild-type heirloom currant tomato collected in Mexico, producing an explosion of pea-sized, intensely sweet-tart red fruits in loose clusters continuously from early summer to frost. The tough little vines shrug off the heat, humidity, and disease pressure that slow down larger-fruited tomatoes, making this one of the most productive and trouble-free tomatoes for Gulf South gardens. Fruits are best picked and eaten straight off the vine or tossed whole into salads, since their small size makes stemming tedious for cooking; a light monthly feeding and consistent watering keep the sprawling plants producing all season.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Trials

common_name: Surfinia Petunia (Original Vigorous Trailing Petunia Series)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after the last frost in full sun with rich, well-drained soil or potting mix; Surfinia trails vigorously over hanging basket edges and window boxes and needs regular feeding to sustain its long, heavy-blooming cascades.

directions: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained soil or a quality potting mix, and feed every one to two weeks through the season since Surfinia's vigorous growth and nonstop bloom draw heavily on nutrients. Introduced by Suntory in Japan in 1989, Surfinia was the original vegetatively propagated trailing petunia series that launched the entire modern spreading-petunia category, valued for cascades that can trail three feet or more and for far better heat, humidity, and rain tolerance than older seed-grown petunias. Unlike many petunias it does not require deadheading to keep blooming, as spent flowers largely self-clean, though a midsummer shearing back by a third refreshes leggy growth and triggers a fresh flush. Its exceptional vigor and weather resistance have made it a longtime standard for hanging baskets, window boxes, and large mixed containers in hot, humid climates.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

common_name: Cora Vinca (Disease-Resistant Heat-Tolerant Annual Vinca Series)

planting.note: Transplant into warm soil a week or two after the last frost once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Cora thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South summer and is one of the few bedding annuals that shrugs off Phytophthora blight in wet soil.

directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid overhead irrigation late in the day since even this disease-resistant series performs best with good air movement around the crown. Cora was bred specifically for strong resistance to Phytophthora and Aerial Blight, the soilborne and foliar diseases that devastate older annual vinca plantings in hot, humid, rainy summers, making it dramatically more reliable than heirloom vinca strains in Gulf Coast beds and highway medians. Once established it is remarkably drought- and heat-tolerant, blooming continuously from late spring through the first frost with almost no deadheading or maintenance required. Its toughness and disease resistance have made it a standard choice for low-input municipal and commercial plantings as well as home landscapes across the Deep South.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Vinca Disease Resistance Trials
